Breaking: ADHD Medications May Help Ease Menopausal Brain Fog

📅 23 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (838 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that medications commonly used to treat attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) may help reduce certain symptoms of menopausal brain fog, according to a review presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of the Menopause Society.
  • The research suggests that both lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) and atomoxetine (Strattera) may improve self-reported executive function in perimenopausal and postmenopausal people.
  • While this scoping review indicated promising results, experts caution that it may be too early to begin recommending these medications to females experiencing menopause.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that medications commonly used to treat attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) may help reduce certain symptoms of menopausal brain fog, according to a review presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of the Menopause Society. The findings have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

The research suggests that both lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) and atomoxetine (Strattera) may improve self-reported executive function in perimenopausal and postmenopausal people. However, they highlighted little to no effect on objective cognitive tests.

While this scoping review indicated promising results, experts caution that it may be too early to begin recommending these medications to females experiencing menopause.

Sara Vaughn, MD, Chief Medical Officer at Clair Health, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings are interesting and hypothesis-generating, but they do not yet establish ADHD medications as a treatment for menopausal brain fog.

Sources indicate that many middle-aged females report experiencing forgetfulness, slow thinking, reduced concentration, and difficulty finding words. This is often referred to as “brain fog,” and is a common occurrence during various stages of menopause.

These symptoms of brain fog also mirror the symptoms of ADHD.

It has been revealed that brain fog may be due to declining or fluctuating levels of estrogen during perimenopause, which affects dopamine and norepinephrine signaling in the prefrontal cortex and the hippocampus. This can impact memory, focus, and executive functioning.

Despite how disruptive these symptoms can be to quality of life, there is presently no medication approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to manage them. This often leaves clinicians in a position of trying to differentiate between brain fog from menopause and undiagnosed ADHD.

The review analyzed five studies involving females ages 45–60 with their last menstrual period within the past 10 years. The studies all focused on how ADHD medications affect outcome measures of cognition and ADHD severity.

The researchers found that with lisdexamfetamine, scores on the Brown Attention Deficit Disorder Scale (BADDS), a self-report rating scale that measures ADHD symptoms, dropped from 35.7 to 21.2, compared with 29.8 with a placebo. With atomoxetine, BADDS scores decreased from 38.6 to 25.5, compared with 30.1 with a placebo.

There was no significant benefit observed on objective cognitive tests (ex., memory and processing speed).

These findings suggest that certain ADHD medications may improve perceived cognitive symptoms during menopause, although benefits were not demonstrated on objective cognitive tests.

Jennifer Tat, a medical student at the University of Tennessee Health Sciences Center and lead author of the study, noted, “In the population data, symptom severity, not a formal ADHD diagnosis, predicted menopausal burden. Many women were never diagnosed, so relying on a chart diagnosis misses the women most at risk.”.

In a recent development, “We have evidence that the menopause transition is associated with measurable brain changes,” said Vaughn. “But no specific brain signature of menopausal brain fog has been established. To study it rigorously, we first need to define what the term means and measure it consistently.”.

Limitations of this review include the small number of studies and the small sample sizes. Most of the measures were also self-reported, which leaves room for error.

Also, the FDA has not approved these types of medications for menopausal brain fog, meaning using them for these purposes would be off-label.

“ADHD medications are not without risks, and I think it is too early to use them routinely for menopausal ‘brain fog,’” mentioned Vaughn.

In a recent development, ADHD medications can carry risks, including cardiovascular side effects. Stimulants such as lisdexamfetamine also have the potential for misuse and dependence. These medications should only be used with medical supervision.

Recent findings suggest that “I am a strong proponent of treating the underlying disorder rather than treating isolated symptoms. ADHD and menopausal cognitive symptoms may look alike, but that does not mean they share the same underlying mechanism—or require the same treatment,” noted Vaughn.

Further research, including additional long-term prospective studies, is needed before clinical guidance can be changed.

“We hope this opens up the conversations with patients and providers. We recommend clinicians to screen patients for ADHD and, for those who screen positive, refer them to our psychiatric colleagues who have the knowledge and resources to perform a diagnostic test so that those women who have gone undiagnosed with ADHD can get the treatment they need and deserve,” stated Tat.

According to the National Council on Aging (NCOA), your brain requires exercise to function optimally, just like your muscles do.

Ways to help keep your brain sharp and manage menopausal brain fog include:.

The NCOA also suggests keeping your brain well-exercised by:.

You can also speak with your healthcare professional about how menopause, estrogen levels, hormone therapy, and modifiable risk factors like a sedentary lifestyle or high blood pressure can affect cognitive health.

Recent findings suggest that “I want clinicians to know that they must take brain fog seriously. Ask whether the symptoms are fresh or a lifelong pattern that menopause has worsened. ADHD in women often goes unrecognized for decades,” said Tat.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dongfeng Nissan officially opened the early order book on its new NX7 hybrid yesterday, promising up to 320 km (~198 miles) of all-electric range from a 40 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery and a $20,000 price tag.

In a recent development, when the first generation Nissan LEAF bowed with 70-ish miles of range from its 24 kWh li-ion battery pack, it struggled to meet widespread adoption, especially in an SUV-obsessed US market that demands forethought-free trips to Home Depot and bladder-busting range. The company’s latest 2027 Rogue Hybrid is a step in the right direction, using a gas engine to generate electricity for a pair of electric drive motors that deliver a driving experience that’s remarkably similar to a “pure” electric car – but without a plug, it’s still entirely dependent on fossil fuels. The new Dongfeng Nissan NX7, though? That’s a different story.

It has been revealed that the plug-in hybrid Dongfeng Nissan NX7 might be called a “long range hybrid” in the same sense that Volvo’s Euro-market XC70 is, in that it’s an EV for the 360-odd days a year that you’re driving less than 200 miles, and an ICE vehicle for the handful of days you drive more. And if you’re one of those people who thinks stopping on road trips is a character flaw, a fully charged and topped off NX7 will take you an astonishing 1,666 km (~1,035 miles) from where you started.

The upcoming NX7 could be an ideal lilypad vehicle for North American drivers who are either too afraid of being caught without a charger or too invested in the outcome of one or more dumb oil wars to confidently make the switch to EV – and, even at twice the 129,900 yuan ($~19,400) asking price, I think it would be a hit.

For that money, NX7 buyers get an absolutely loaded Model Y-sized crossover (they’re within 1/4″ of each other in length), with a 17.3″ central touchscreen, a fully digital instrument cluster, and (on higher-spec models) a positively massive 55″ augmented-reality head-up display powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8295P automotive processor and running on Nissan OS 3.0 with an AI-powered voice assistant developed with iFlytek that, Nissan claims, can recognize natural-language commands, remember user preferences, and even recognize occupants, adjusting vehicle settings accordingly.

In a recent development, on top-shelf models, the NX7 cabins get “AI Zero-Pressure Cloud Blanket” seats that use sensors and air-cushion arrays to dynamically adjust for maximum comfort, and include heating, ventilation, and a 12-point SPA-level massage function. The front seats can be fully reclined to create a bed-like configuration that will be familiar to Cube owners. The NX7 even offers an on-board refrigerator and motion-sickness prevention system that Nissan claims can reduce motion sickness by as much as 83% (which, like, I wouldn’t want to be the one to test that – but seems cool).

Power comes from a 1.5-liter naturally aspirated internal combustion engine making 98 hp that’s paired to a 228 hp electric drive motor and the previously mentioned 40.9 kWh LFP battery. It’s not immediately clear if the NX7 uses a conventional parallel hybrid system like a Prius or a series-hybrid-plus-plug setup, but Dongfeng’s hybrid technology patents describe a pretty versatile arrangement with four possible operating modes: series hybrid, parallel hybrid, direct engine drive and electricity generation – which means the vehicle can theoretically use the ICE motor as a generator, drive the wheels mechanically, or work alongside the electric motor, depending on what the operating conditions call for. Whether any or all four modes make it to production on the NX7 remains to be seen, but it’s an intriguing bit of engineering for a vehicle promising nearly 200 miles of electric driving range.

Sources indicate that why is this article written like it will be available in the US market? It’s made in China and has Chinese software, we’ll never see it.

The final production version will be shown to the public for the first time at the Guangzhou Auto Show later this month, but you can let us know what you think of the fresh NX7 in the comments, today.

The Mini 3 can even send images, use voice commands in various languages, pair up with your smartphone, and send emergency notes 24/7. Oh, and it’s tough as nails, has a strong battery, and can even set you up with the weather forecast.

Recent findings suggest that here’s a pair for the trail-running novice and seasoned vet alike. The shoe combines comfort, support, durability, and a decidedly stylish look that has no trouble gobbling up mile after mile on the dusty (or muddy, or rocky) trail. On the surface, you get some serious colorways and a toothy but not over-the-top look. Under the hood, an improved midsole that rebounds like an NBA-level power forward and dual mid-foot webbing reinforcements to assist those active feet. And the details add up, from the padded collar to the stay-in-place tongue wings, making for a smooth trek even way, way down (or up) the trail.

Industry observers note that what takes a hoodie into the high-performance echelon and helps it excel there? Extremely breathable and temperature-regulating fleece, genuine ripstop shell fabric, and a pair of warming pockets. Oh, and the raglan sleeves and elastic ends keep things comfortable and secure the warmth. It’s an added bonus that the fit is just about perfect, the hood wears brilliantly, and the whole thing can fend off even the thickest brush and snags. As Marmot rightfully claims, this one breathes like a feather and feels like a fleece. Usually it’s one or the other but not here. Gift this one to that restless outdoorsy soul who stays active year-round.

Sources indicate that taking the enhanced vision category into the unexpected realm of cool, Nocs is up to good work. The latest binocular set fits the bill, with powerful lenses and a textured design that’s easy to carry (and even easier on the eyes). Waterproof, they can accompany any trek, on land or water, in summer or winter, and that goes for all types of outdoors enthusiasts, from casual birders and hikers to backcountry pros and road trippers who like to hit the pullouts and take it all in. Compact with full-size clarity, these binocs do what many twice their size try to do, so store ’em in a small pack or wear ‘em over your neck with ease.

In a recent development, flannels are a staple in an outdoorsman's wardrobe. If he has yet to try Outerknown's Blanket Shirt, now is the time to gift him one. They come in a ton of colors and are woven in a way that has just the right warmth and softness, without ever going too extreme. Call it the Goldilocks flannel.

Industry observers note that you really can’t miss with a trusty multitool. And there’s no more trusty versions out there than the Skeletool CX from Leatherman. It’s lightweight at just five ounces and sports seven different tools: a steel blade, pliers, wire cutters, a customizable bit driver, and a dual carabiner/bottle opener. That’ll serve anyone’s everyday needs pretty well.

We love this new book from Max Humphrey, a real celebration of all things Yellowstone. Unlike many coffee table books, this one makes you feel like you’re actually sharing a car with the author and touring the Park, taking in great panoramas of lodges, bison jams, mountain vistas, and more. Perhaps that’s the attention to details and fresh perspective you get from an interior designer like Humphrey. If you like this one, consider his other book on the Great Smoky Mountains.

Industry observers note that if they're a runner, they're going to need a few things to continue that before-or-after-work pursuit during the winter months. A headlamp is one of those items, as dark runs need light. The latest offering from BioLite is super light at 2.6 ounces, has a comfortable strap, and holds a ton of charge at 200 hours of runtime. And the best part? I haven't had it shaking or bouncing on me once yet.

Read More: Best Gifts for Camping.

Even if he's a man of the woods, AllTrails is a great app to gift him. The Plus membership provides offline maps (more than 450,000 trails around the world), 3D trail previews, and wrong turn alerts. Plus, there's the community aspect of the app where he can log hikes live and earn badges.

It has been revealed that when it comes to hard coolers, there are few that do it better than RTIC. The brand's 52-quart wheeled version is a lightweight, uncompromising hauler that can house 78 cans and keep contents cold for up to five days. The all-terrain, puncture-proof tires ensure that his camp meals and drinks know no bounds.

Ryan Brower is the Senior Gear and Reviews Editor at Men’s Health, where he tests the best products in outdoor gear, tech, running shoes, and more. Industry News: China’s electric airliner era starts with a 19-seat plane and 400 km of range

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (884 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • COMAC’s CE-25A, China’s 19-seat battery-electric commuter plane, flew with a crew for the first time on Saturday in Binzhou, Shandong.
  • In a recent development, it wasn’t the plane’s first flight.
  • According to recent reports, the CE-25A is a T-tail commuter plane with 10 electric ducted fans on the wings, five per side, instead of propellers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

COMAC’s CE-25A, China’s 19-seat battery-electric commuter plane, flew with a crew for the first time on Saturday in Binzhou, Shandong. Two pilots and a flight test engineer were aboard the roughly 10-tonne demonstrator, and COMAC claims every system worked normally.

In a recent development, it wasn’t the plane’s first flight. The CE-25A had already completed 19 autonomous test flights with nobody on board since February 2, and China’s aviation regulator is now reviewing it for a type certificate.

According to recent reports, the CE-25A is a T-tail commuter plane with 10 electric ducted fans on the wings, five per side, instead of propellers. COMAC lists a 300 km/h cruise speed and a 400 km (250-mile) range.

Sources indicate that the CAAC accepting COMAC’s type certificate application starts the airworthiness review. It doesn’t mean paying passengers are close, and COMAC hasn’t given a date for commercial service.

The program has been quiet for a long time. COMAC demonstrated a CE-25A model at the China International Import Expo in Shanghai in November 2023, with a placard listing 400 to 500 km of range and a 400 km/h top cruise speed. The full-size aircraft, registered B-0EFH, only became public when photos leaked on Chinese social media on October 28.

Recent findings suggest that the obvious battery candidate is CATL. In July 2023, COMAC, CATL, and Shanghai Jiao Tong University formed a joint venture with CNY 600 million in registered capital to develop electric aircraft, as we reported when CATL debuted its aviation unit.

It has been revealed that CATL had just unveiled its “condensed” battery at the time, claiming up to 500 Wh/kg at the cell level, and mentioned it was testing the cells to aviation standards. Neither manufacturer has confirmed what’s inside the CE-25A, though.

~500 Wh/kg has long been seen as the target for battery energy density to enable electric flight on a commercial scale.

COMAC isn’t alone in flying a large electric demonstrator. In August, Heart Aerospace flew its X1 in Plattsburgh, Fresh York, for 27 minutes. It’s a 25,000-lb aircraft with a 106-foot wingspan, which Heart calls the largest battery-electric aircraft ever flown.

Eviation flew its 9-passenger Alice back in September 2022, then laid off most of its staff in early 2025.

Heart is the closest Western comparison. It dropped its 19-seat ES-19 for the 30-seat ES-30 back in 2022, and the ES-30 now relies on reserve turbogenerators to stretch its range, with BAE Systems working on the battery. Heart is targeting 2031 for service and claims “more than 40%” lower operating costs.

For years, the go-to excuse in the West for doing nothing about emissions was China. Why should we bother, the argument went, if China won’t? Now China is pulling ahead, and it’s doing it by cutting its dependence on fossil fuels.

Look at trucking. Electric trucks hit 50.3% of China’s heavy truck sales in September, and they’re already eating into the country’s diesel demand. In the US, electric models were about 0.3% of heavy-truck sales last year, according to the ICCT.

A great step in the right direction, probably needs a doubling in range but at current rates of progress that will only be five years away.

According to recent reports, now it’s planes, starting where batteries make sense today: short regional routes. The CE-25A’s 400 km shrinks once you keep the reserves regulators require, and a Beechcraft 1900 turboprop in the same class covers well over 1,000 km. So it’s not replacing turboprops anytime soon. But that’s how trucking started too. Short-haul first, then long-haul tractors once the batteries caught up.

And this couldn’t happen fast enough. We’re in the middle of a diesel and jet fuel crisis. Jet fuel averaged $3.50 a gallon in early August, up 63% from a year earlier, according to Heart Aerospace. Every truck and plane China moves to batteries is one less exposed to that.

It has been revealed that china also has the batteries to pull it off, with CATL in the joint venture. Meanwhile, Heart has pushed to 2031 and added a fuel-burning backup, and Eviation is a cautionary tale.

With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. #121353. The Simple Guide to Finding a Weighted Vest You’ll Actually Use

📅 02 Nov 2019 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3599 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Womenshealthmag ↗ Open Full Page

The Simple Guide to Finding a Weighted Vest You’ll Actually Use

📅 02 Nov 2019 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3599 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in.
  • Slip on a weighted vest, and suddenly your regular walk, chores, or bodyweight exercises feel a little more rewarding—the extra weight offering a simple boost in effort and making us more aware of the way our bodies maintain balance and stability.
  • It has been revealed that I’m a certified personal trainer, and I sometimes recommend weighted vests to older adult clients as a way to add extra challenge to walking, cardio, and bodyweight exercises.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Slip on a weighted vest, and suddenly your regular walk, chores, or bodyweight exercises feel a little more rewarding—the extra weight offering a simple boost in effort and making us more aware of the way our bodies maintain balance and stability.

It has been revealed that I’m a certified personal trainer, and I sometimes recommend weighted vests to older adult clients as a way to add extra challenge to walking, cardio, and bodyweight exercises. While recent research suggests that weighted vests may not have a dramatic impact on bone density, they’re still a safe and convenient way to increase the load on your muscles and joints, helping you push yourself a little harder than usual.

According to recent reports, weighted vests let you add extra resistance to walking, stair climbing, jumping, push-ups, and pull-ups without needing to grip dumbbells or barbells. Some clients even wear them during everyday activities like cleaning, yard work, or mowing the lawn—making fitness a little more functional and, yes, a bit more fun.

That remarked, if you’ve been diagnosed with osteoporosis, consult your doctor before adding a weighted vest to your exercise routine, while folks who are pregnant or experience back, neck, or joint pain should also avoid them.

In a recent development, before you take the plunge on purchasing a weighted vest, you should consider the resistance level, workouts such as walking or HIIT, and whether materials are sweat-resistant to determine which one is best for you. Ready to get vested?

After testing a handful of weighted vests for weeks, the trophy goes to the Omorpho G-Vest for its remarkable comfort, ideal weight, and sleek design. I spent a week wearing it for my regular lifting sessions and hour-long walks. It’s easy to wear for my normal gym routine, which includes moves such as walking lunges, Copenhagen planks, pull-ups, and push-ups.

However, I found it to be challenging when worn for heavier compound lifts like front squats, deadlifts, and barbell rows. Other than walking lunges, I wouldn’t normally add load to those exercises because of the logistics of holding or hanging weight, but the vest makes it possible to add resistance without gripping anything.

The fit is another reason the G-Vest earns the top spot. This vest is surprisingly comfortable considering it weighs just over five pounds from stainless steel balls. While the back panels have more weight—226 stainless steel balls on the back and 122 on the front—the weight distribution feels uniform when wearing.

It has been revealed that it’s also compact—from the shoulder straps to the bottom of the vest is about 17 inches, which, for me, is great since I have a very short torso. It also doesn't dig into the top of my hip bone when I move around.

Recent findings suggest that even if you don’t have a short torso, you’ll still appreciate the soft-to-the-touch polyester fabric, despite it feeling like neoprene (synthetic rubber). I use adjustable cords at the sides for a customized fit. There are also straps on the shoulders to accommodate a wider frame, or if you want the vest to sit a little lower on your torso. For reference, I have mine on the shortest setting.

One downside of the G-Vest is its limited size options. There are only two: S/M or L/XL. I highly recommend using the size chart to determine which fit is best for you. I’m typically a medium when shopping for athletic tops, but I chose the L/XL because my chest circumference is on the cusp of both options. It’s also worth mentioning that the weight of the S/M vest is four pounds and 12 ounces, while the L/XL is five pounds and six ounces.

Read More: Omorpho G-Vest Review.

You can shell out up to $300 for a weighted vest, but not everyone needs all the extra features that come with that higher price tag. The ApexUp weighted vest is a popular option thanks to its low price point, but it offers more than just savings.

According to recent reports, this vest is built from neoprene (which is the durable synthetic rubber you’ll find in wetsuits) and filled with iron sand, a material that’s denser than natural sand and absorbs less moisture. As a result, it won’t stick to you or clump up when you sweat.

Industry observers note that it has a smooth, comfortable feel, with seams that are stitched over with fabric to prevent rubbing and chafing. Wide armholes and an adjustable strap across the chest mean you can get a comfortable fit, no matter your chest size.

Industry observers note that the solo strap in ApexUp’s 10-pound version means it’s more likely to shift around during dynamic movements like burpees, making this vest a better choice for things like walking. A lot of the weight in the vest is in the front straps, so just be aware of your posture while you use this. But the mesh storage pocket in back is secure and roomy enough for your phone, which is a nice feature if you want to free up your hands.

Sources indicate that A common complaint with this vest is the smell, which may be due to that neoprene cover. If you notice it and it bothers you, just let the vest air out a little before using it. Also, be aware that the ApexUp vest doesn’t allow you to tack on extra weight. But at this low price, you can simply buy a latest one when you’re ready for more resistance and still come out on top, price-wise.

The best weighted vest is one you’ll actually wear, and the Stakt Adjustable Weighted Vest makes that part easy. Instead of looking like tactical gear, its streamlined neoprene construction fits close to the body and feels more like a weighted garment.

One way WH fitness and reviews editor Natascha Grief, NASM-CPT likes to use weighted vests in her own training and with her training clients is to increase proprioception, or awareness of the body’s position in space. Because the Stakt vest distributes weight around the torso instead of loading only the shoulders, it can provide helpful feedback for connecting with the core and postural muscles during movement.

Recent findings suggest that the Stakt weighted vest starts at six pounds and a two-pound zip-on extension brings it up to eight pounds. Grief tested both configurations while walking, doing chores around her apartment, doing pushups, and adding it to a functional training workout. It delivered comfortable, evenly distributed weight that fits and feels more like an additional clothing layer than a traditional weighted vest.

The aluminum front buckles feel sturdy. The shoulder straps use a hook-and-loop adjustment system, so once Grief found the right adjustment, it was a set-it-and-forget-it situation, and the straps stayed put. “I didn’t have to interrupt any workout to readjust them,” she said.

A porous mesh liner creates a comfortable buffer between the body and the neoprene, which adds some breathability. It also zips out for washing, which is a helpful feature, especially considering that this vest is worn close to the body. The vest also has a mesh pocket for small essentials. Its reflective detailing is minimal though, so you’ll want additional visibility gear when walking in low-light conditions.

Read More: Stakt Weighted Vest Review.

If you’re looking for an adjustable-weight option ideal for specific functional training exercises and rucking, the Hyper Vest Elite from Hyperwear is highly customizable. I tested the 10-pound model, which is weighted with 66 individual 2.25-ounce stainless steel bars, each with its own little pocket.

If you prefer heavier weights, 15- and 20-pound options are available. Plus, you can purchase a box of individual weights to load up your vest (each pocket can fit two 2.25-ounce weights).

In a recent development, I wore it during multiple 60-minute walks, squats, pull-ups, push-ups, and back extensions. With the full 10 pounds loaded on my body, I found it really difficult to do pull-ups and push-ups. However, when I removed some of the weights from the individual pockets, it made for a more manageable load.

That said, I’m not sure how realistic it is to load up these tiny weights into individual pouches when switching between exercises. I think it’s a great feature, but personally, I’d design my workouts to ensure I didn’t have to adjust the weights more than once.

In a recent development, there are adjustable cords on each side to cinch or loosen for your preferred fit, but you won’t find shoulder strap adjustments like on the Omorpho vests. I also noticed the Hyperwear vest sits nearly five inches lower on my torso than the Omorpho vest. It doesn’t dig into my hips, but I notice it grazes my lower back when walking. It’s not a deal breaker, but I prefer shorter styles. Four size options are available: small, medium, large, and extra large.

As for material, I appreciate the heavy-duty construction of this vest, which is made with Cordura, a synthetic, tear-resistant fabric popular for backpacks and military clothing. It will hold up for years, even if you proposal to go hiking or wear it in the elements. I also like the reflective strips at the zipper and across the chest for increased visibility outdoors.

If you’re looking for a weighted vest with resistance that pushes your limits while not disrupting your range of motion, this one by Vivitory checks the box. Despite the non-cropped fit, it still stays in place with only two adjustable straps and distributes weight evenly (11 pounds for the medium size and 18 pounds for the large size).

It has been revealed that WH art director Christine Giordano was pleasantly surprised by how light it felt compared to holding it. “I was nervous it was going to be too heavy for me or cause pain in my lower back, but I was wrong,” says Giordano. “It didn’t bounce up and down or move all over—it stayed snug to my body while not being too hot and bulky.”.

In a recent development, she loves wearing it during easy walks when waiting around for her kids’ sporting events or for more intense workouts, such as CrossFit or burpees. “I’m not a huge fan of dumbbell step-ups, so I tried it with the vest for the added weight without leaning forward,” she indicates.

Recent findings suggest that as for the material, it’s made with neoprene, a synthetic rubber resistant to sweat that Giordano says she found to be breathable. There are also reflective strips on the vest for visibility during dawn or dusk, and a small pouch at the back for holding essentials.

In a recent development, if you get seriously sweaty during cardio or weightlifting, this 12-pound Reebok weighted vest is an option in hot summer temps. The back has a breathable ventilation panel that allows air to circulate.

Sources indicate that WH contributor Korin Miller has recently added it to her workout gear lineup. “I like to go hard with my workouts, and I get really sweaty as a result—I appreciate the open-air design of this vest so I can cool off,” notes Miller. “That, combined with the airy fabric, means I won’t end up with the vest sticking against my skin during workouts.”.

Aside from its sweat-wicking properties, its two adjustable straps allow for a customized fit during a variety of workouts. For Miller, specifically walking, cycling, rowing, and bodyweight movements, such as planks and squats.

But, it’s important to note this model isn’t ideal for jumping. “Those extra weights can flap around during bigger movements like running and HIIT workouts—basically anything that has you jumping up and down,” says Miller.

Read More: Reebok Weighted Vest Review.

The Omorpho G-Vest Icon is a quality choice for runners and HIIT workouts, given its snug fit and moderate weight that doesn’t feel like too much. The design is really similar to Omorpho’s OG model, with soft neoprene-style fabric, stainless steel ball bearings embedded into the fabric, and waist and shoulder adjustments for a custom fit.

The main difference is the adjustable weight and reflective strips throughout for extra visibility during night runs. The adjustable weight system is genius. It involves “G-Packs” of varying weights that snap in and out, allowing you to tack on additional, evenly distributed weight fast. (Just a heads up: A set of three G-Packs that brings the weight up to 12 pounds costs an extra $129.).

We also like that the encased stainless steel weights are not featured through the chest area. If you want to wear the G-Vest Icon with just a sports bra, you won’t have any irritation from high-impact movements.

For reference, the weights go up the entirety of the front panels on the men’s version. While the vest’s fitted style is ideal for runs, its six-pound weight means it’s better suited for things like short runs and sprints.

According to recent reports, one downside is that the neoprene-style fabric made our tester sweat a ton when worn with layers. “My first experience with the vest was under my winter jacket on a 10-degree day during an hour-long walk,” WH contributor Korin Miller notes. “I sweat my butt off despite the cold temperatures, compared to having sweat evaporate from my skin at the gym.”.

Read More: Omorpho G-Vest Icon Review.

It has been revealed that besides being a WH Fitness Awards 2025 winner, the Empower Weighted Vest is the only vest we’ve seen with a cross-style fit. It’s designed specifically to fit women’s curves while offering supreme support for the shoulder blades. The fit is compact with less material at the sides, while the straps are fully adjustable.

While its main highlight is being a custom fit for women, another unique feature is six removable one-pound bags (three in the front and three in the back pockets). In the 10-pound model (weight ranges from eight to 16 pounds), the vest can go as low as four pounds when the weights are removed if you’re seeking only light resistance.

Recent findings suggest that WH health and fitness editor Addison Aloian, NASM-CPT, uses it for taking her workouts to the next level. “It elevates my walks, helps my core activate more, and makes my bodyweight exercises harder,” she says. Her only complaint is that the removable weights can make it feel bulky and interfere with hitting the full range of motion with a handful of exercises. “If I wanted to do crunches, I couldn’t lie on my back without it arching, and I couldn’t do supermans from my stomach because the bags in the front made it so I couldn’t lie flat,” she says. “During other strength exercises like squats, it hit the top of my thigh and prevented me from moving down further.” Perhaps it’s best to use the added pocket weights only during walks.

As for material, it’s neoprene for optimal sweat resistance, like the Vivitory and Prodigen weighted vests.

It has been revealed that not everyone wants or needs the 20-pound resistance TRX’s Hexgrip Weighted Vest can offer. But this vest is adjustable, allowing you to tweak the weight in one-pound increments, giving you room to grow up to that 20 pounds. So, if you want to use it as a 10-pound vest to start, more power to you.

This sturdy vest helps you get a secure fit with the help of three wide Velcro straps, making it a solid option for dynamic movements, some cardio workouts, and general strength training. The neoprene inner is comfortable against your skin, while the snug fit and smartly positioned weights mean you don’t have to stress about the vest moving around on you while you work out.

Recent findings suggest that while it’s on the heavier end, it’s not bulky. As a result, you can still feel comfortable doing your usual range of motion. Just a heads up: Some of the weights are positioned across the chest, which may feel more noticeable if you have larger breasts. But those adjustable straps mean you can lower or raise the shoulder straps to find a position that’s more comfortable for you.

In a recent development, the weights slip into individual pockets to prevent them from shifting around, but make sure they’re secured well before you start your workout. (Some people have reported them sliding out.) Because the adjustment process takes some time, this isn’t a vest you’ll want to adjust mid-workout. This vest also comes in a 40-pound version, although most exercisers will do best with the 20-pounder as a heavy option.

If you have broader shoulders, the RITFIT has fully adjustable straps. They're spaced further apart—one sits higher on your chest and the other closer to your waist.

It has been revealed that it can be more comfortable if you have a larger chest, while it may run bigger on smaller frames. It also has mesh pockets to store your keys and phone.

Industry observers note that the load on a weighted vest can range from 3 to over 30 pounds, depending on the style and brand. If you’ve never used a weighted vest or are new to resistance training, I recommend starting with a lighter option between 3 and 10 pounds. Our best overall pick is optimal for newbies since it’s five pounds.

Heavier vests are ideal for loading bodyweight exercises like push-ups, pull-ups, squats, and walking lunges. They can also be used for walking, hiking, or rucking, depending on your fitness level. Lighter vests are ideal for speed training like sprinting, interval training, and plyometric exercises like box jumps, burpees, or jump roping.

Sources indicate that durable materials such as Cordura, nylon, and polyester are less likely to tear from constant wear during intense movement. All of the picks on this list are made from either of these three fabrics, and I found they perform well during explosive workouts and cardio. They also wick away sweat, which is a must for ultimate comfort. As for fit, I love an adjustable closure system with a zipper or buckles at the front, waist, and shoulders for customizing the fit.

Since 2020, we’ve updated this story and tested every major weighted vest on the market. I’m a certified personal trainer with the National Strength and Conditioning Association. I’ve worked in the health and fitness industry for nine years and have six years of hands-on experience working with clients one-on-one and in small group settings. With experience testing and reviewing hundreds of fitness products over the years, I wore select weighted vests for multiple hour-long walks and workouts, including exercises like push-ups, pull-ups, lunges, planks, and box jumps. I paid close attention to the material to see how it held up against sweat, fit for comfort, and weight for resistance levels. I also kept notes of my likes and dislikes.

‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’: Inside the Psychedelic 1970s-Inspired Dystopian Sets

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1786 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that francis Lawrence, director of The Hunger Games, has a tradition with author Suzanne Collins.
  • Lawrence’s latest adaptation, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping (in theaters today), returns to Panem, a postapocalyptic nation where the ruling Capitol controls twelve districts through extreme systemic oppression—most notoriously the titular spectacle in which children are selected by lottery and forced to fight to the death in an arena.
  • District 12’s female tribute Maysilee Donner (McKenna Grace) at the reaping.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that francis Lawrence, director of The Hunger Games, has a tradition with author Suzanne Collins. Before bringing a new installment of her bestselling dystopian saga to the massive screen, the two join forces to envision how the fictional world of Panem will take shape. “I go to New York each time, and we sit in a conference room at Scholastic,” claims Lawrence, who has directed five of the franchise’s six films. “We go through the book page by page and beat out what we think the movie is going to look like.”.

Lawrence’s latest adaptation, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping (in theaters today), returns to Panem, a postapocalyptic nation where the ruling Capitol controls twelve districts through extreme systemic oppression—most notoriously the titular spectacle in which children are selected by lottery and forced to fight to the death in an arena. Set twenty-four years before the original The Hunger Games (2012) plotline, the prequel follows District 12’s sixteen-year-old Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada)—the future mentor (played by Woody Harrelson) to Katniss Everdeen (Jennifer Lawrence) and Peeta Mellark (Josh Hutcherson)—as he is selected to fight in the Second Quarter Quell, a particularly sadistic rendition of the Games held every twenty-five years.

District 12’s female tribute Maysilee Donner (McKenna Grace) at the reaping.

Though the dystopia is set in a future North America, the previous prequel, The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes (2023), drew from the architecture of 1940s and ’50s postwar Berlin to depict evil President Snow’s rise to tyranny. Set forty years later, Sunrise explores Panem at a new stage of its evolution. Designed by returning production designer Uli Hanisch, the film follows Haymitch from his impoverished mining district, which barely evolves throughout the series’s sixty-five year timeline, to the opulent Capitol, whose extravagance is expressed through a 1970s-inflected visual lexicon.

“I realized the ’70s fall right smack in the middle between that movie and the originals, so we could lean into that,” says Lawrence. Hanisch and his team incorporated references to Andy Warhol, Studio 54, and the decade’s psychedelic color palette, appropriating its progressive spirit to convey the Capitol’s opulence and authoritarianism—and, particularly in the arena, using the aesthetic as a means of deception. “To turn the ’70s style from something progressive, liberal, young, and open-minded into something evil is a twist,” says Hanisch. “But that is the key to the entire film’s design.”.

Industry observers note that haymitch and Maysilee as allies in the arena. The forest portion was filmed separately near Cologne, Germany.

According to recent reports, the stylistic choice is also a poignant nod to Collins’s original inspiration for the book series. The 1970s marked a transformation in American television: as color TVs became ubiquitous in households across the country, sporting spectacles, variety shows, and beauty pageants flourished, establishing cultural touchstones that would help shape the contemporary reality programming Collins critiques and satirizes in The Hunger Games. “I was flipping through the channels one night between reality television programs and actual footage of the Iraq War, when the idea came to me,” Collins recalled in a 2018 interview with The Fresh York Times. The juxtaposition inspired her to explore just-war theory for young people through an authoritarian dystopia in which mass entertainment is an instrument of political control.

From an abandoned rural steel mill to authoritarian monuments from postwar Berlin, the film draws on politically charged German sites to capture Panem at a pivotal stage in its political and architectural evolution.

According to recent reports, production Designer Uli Hanisch at the District 12 set. “District 12 is the most sentimental set to me because I’d known this site near my hometown my entire life,” Hanisch states.

To recreate the Appalachian-inspired, deteriorating industrial landscape of District 12 that was shot in Atlanta in the original series, the production utilized a sprawling abandoned steel mill in Duisburg, Germany, Hanisch’s hometown. “I wish we had it in the original movies, because it is an unbelievable space,” Lawrence says of the post-industrial, rural landscape, which also appeared in The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, Hanisch’s first film in the franchise. “Everywhere you look is exactly how I have always imagined District 12.”.

While District 12 was filmed near Atlanta in the original films, director Francis Lawrence’s fascination with German architecture brought production to Berlin for The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes. It was there that he began collaborating with Berlin-based production designer Hanisch, who proposed this steel mill nearby his hometown for the newly introduced location. Upon seeing photographs, Lawrence exclaimed, “Are you kidding me? ... Let’s go tomorrow,” and promptly flew out to see it for himself.

The production designer added modest huts at the edge of a nearby quarry to recreate the Seam, home to Haymitch, his girlfriend Lenore Dove (Whitney Peak), and fellow tribute Louella McCoy (Molly McCann), its humble dwellings contrasting the more prosperous merchant district inhabited by fellow tribute Maysilee Donner (Mckenna Grace).

Sources indicate that “Unlike the Capitol, District 12 doesn't evolve stylistically throughout the films. Nobody is investing in it, and everything is gradually deteriorating,” Hanisch explains. The vivid purples and oranges of the Capitol’s ‘70s palette are notably absent, only appearing prominently in propaganda decorating the reaping square, including Hunger Games campaign materials and posters portraying Snow as Panem’s number-one Peacekeeper.

Druscilla in the Capitol before the tribute interviews, which is broadcast to all of Panem.

In a recent development, in the Capitol, however, the architecture takes on a distinctly ‘70s flair. Rooted in the Roman concept of panem et circenses, or “bread and circuses,” from which Panem takes its name, the architecture reinforces the government’s manipulation through spectacle. In the background is Berlin's International Congress Centrum, a colossal, aluminum-clad convention center that opened in 1979, which Lawrence describes as “Cold War-era Berlin showing off in a modern way.” As West Berlin’s most expensive postwar building, the futuristic complex was publicly subsidised to showcase economic prosperity and technological advancement—an evocative backdrop for the Capitol’s own display of authoritarianism.

Sources indicate that “It’s a time of peace for the Capitol with no rebel attacks, so Snow's had time to build the city up in a way that is an extravagant show of power,” Lawrence explains. The chariot parade, which introduces the tributes before the Games, similarly unfolds against the historically-charged Berlin Olympiastadion, which was designed by Werner March for the 1936 Olympics under Nazi Germany to project state power and an illusion of timeless permanence.

According to recent reports, the upstairs library in Plutarch’s home, which he inherited from the Heavensbee dynasty. Reflecting the Capitol’s classic style, it contrasts the Plutarch’s modern downstairs salon which features Warhol-inspired portraits, including one of director Lawrence.

According to recent reports, the Capitol's grandeur is also exhibited inside the mansion of Plutarch Heavensbee (Jesse Plemons), a cameraman with historic ties to Panem’s ruling class. “This was one of my favorite sets because of the scope and scale” Lawrence indicates, noting how its excess reflects the dynasty's immense wealth. Filmed at Berlin's late-1960s modernist Congress Center, the circular residence required twenty-five vans of retro-modern furniture to fill it. The salon, decked in vibrant 1970s furnishings and Warhol-inspired art, showcases Plutarch's modern sensibilities, in stark contrast to the upstairs library inherited from his family. “We wanted to distinguish Plutarch from the dynasty he comes from,” Lawrence explains, reflecting on how the expansive volumes must be a facade of intellectual sophistication.

The set decoration department spent weeks hand-folding and assembling thousands of hollow cardboard books, interspersed with real volumes, including a collection of Edgar Allan Poe’s poetry, which Plutarch references to Haymitch. “We imagined Plutarch might actually be the first Heavensbee to read some of those books,” Hanisch states. “He even says the library is one of the few worthwhile things his ancestors accomplished.”.

Recent findings suggest that the library's custom-built curved bookshelves envelope the characters, symbolising the insularity of Capitol society. “Circles represent both inclusion and exclusion,” Hanisch says. “If you are in the circle, you're in. And if you're not, you're out.” As fans of the franchise will know, Plutarch (originally played by Philip Seymour Hoffman) later reveals himself as a double agent and leader of the underground rebellion against Snow’s regime.

The aspect ratio expands as Haymitch ascends into the eye-shaped arena, emphasizing the landscape’s immersive scale and beauty. While scouting locations, Lawrence drew inspiration from the dramatic landscapes in Terrence Malick’s A Hidden Life. “I had that in my head, only it was a little trippier. The Asturias were perfect,” he recalls. The kaleidoscopic design also inspired the official logo of the 50th Hunger Games, extending the arena’s psychedelic imagery into the Capitol’s propaganda.

The Quarter Quell arena, in particular, embodies the surreal, fantastical ethos of the 1970s that permeates the film, illustrating how the Capitol exploits beauty to disguise its underlying manipulation and brutality. “As I was reading with Suzanne, I said there was an Alice in Wonderland-like element to it, which made me think of the song ‘White Rabbit,’ which made me think of the late ’60s, early ’70s,” Lawrence recalls. “That kind of broke something open for me.”.

Designed in the shape of an eye, the eight to ten mile arena serves as a metaphor for the Capitol's omnipresent surveillance. A golden Cornucopia forms its pupil; vibrant meadows its iris; and the surrounding mountain ranges its whites. In the book, Haymitch describes the especially lethal arena masquerading as an idyllic landscape as a “poisonous beauty of an arena.”.

Lawrence and Haymitch in the arena. The physical flowers were concentrated in the foreground, while visual effects extended the colorful landscape into the distance.

In a recent development, seeking to capture as much natural landscape as possible, Hanisch and location manager Klaus große Darrelmann discovered a remote valley in Asturias, Spain, surrounded by the Cantabrian Mountains. Transforming the isolated valley into a psychedelic paradise proved an enormous undertaking.“The arena was our nemesis,” says Hanisch, recalling how the production had to bring extensive resources to the remote terrain. “You can't even imagine how far away it was or how hard it was to get to.” Crews spent weeks individually installing hundreds of thousands of artificial flowers throughout the meadows and forests.

Despite the arena’s dreamlike beauty, water sources, flowers, and vegetation conceal deadly poisons. “It’s the most colorful and playful dystopia you’ll ever see,” producer Nina Jacobson claims. Perhaps more than anywhere else in Panem, the arena encapsulates how the Capitol weaponizes the electric zeitgeist of the ‘70s as an instrument of control. “To have something so overwhelmingly beautiful and seductive but poisonous and deadly is very cruel,” Hanisch says. “That contradiction captures the mentality of Panem at this point in its history.”.

High altitude, bitter cold, zero drivers: autonomous trucks take on Tibetan mine

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Finding qualified equipment operators is hard enough for most mining companies, and the extreme weather, punishing conditions, and oxygen-deprived air of the Tibetan mountains combine to make finding operators even tougher for the operators if this high-altitude copper mine – but SANY thinks they have a solution: fully self-driving haul trucks.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Finding qualified equipment operators is hard enough for most mining companies, and the extreme weather, punishing conditions, and oxygen-deprived air of the Tibetan mountains combine to make finding operators even tougher for the operators if this high-altitude copper mine – but SANY thinks they have a solution: fully self-driving haul trucks.

According to recent reports, chinese equipment brand SANY has deployed fully 60 of its 70-tonne (~80 ton) payload-rated SKT105ED battery electric haul trucks at the Zhibula Copper Mine in Tibet. Operated by Zijin Minig and Tibet Julong Copper, the mine functions at a dizzying 17,700 foot elevation in a region of the Gangdese Mountains known as the Kailas Range, and the conditions there would challenge the health and safety of even the toughest and fittest operators.

“High-altitude illness becomes increasingly relevant above 2,500 meters,” explains Eacon, in one section of a published paper. “Research involving workers in Andes mines operating between 3,800 and 4,500 meters found that 73% of workers assessed experienced periods of nocturnal oxygen saturation below 85% during their high-altitude shifts, indicating moderate-to-severe hypoxemia.”.

That’s bad news for Zijin’s workers – but the good news here, of course, is that the manufacturer won’t be needing many heavy haul drivers going forward.

SANY has been working with Perth, Australia-based Eacon Mining Technology to develop an autonomous haulage solution that uses a full suite of both in-vehicle and ground-based sensors, adaptive vehicle controls, and machine learning that can handle the massive bad trucks even here in the Kailas range.

“Autonomous haulage offers one way to address this challenge,” continues the Econ report. “Rather than requiring a driver for each truck, autonomous systems allow fleets to be managed through centralized supervision, with personnel overseeing operations and intervening when required. This reduces the need for people to spend entire shifts operating equipment at elevation, while changing how workforce resources are allocated across the mine … depending on the system configuration, some operations can manage autonomous fleets from remote Integrated Operations Centers located away from the mine site, (allowing) personnel to supervise haulage activities from lower-altitude locations, further reducing the need for workers to remain in extreme-altitude environments.”.

The working partnership between the two companies combines SANY’s battery-powered truck platform with Eacon’s full technology stack to create dependable, driverless haul trucks with logic and behaviors that are ideally suited to China’s open-pit mining environments.

Eacon technology is at the moment operating more than 3,100 autonomous trucks cross more than 40 large-scale mines, including Zijin Mining’s Zijinshan Gold-Copper Mine and at the Norton Gold Fields project in Australia.

While specifications for this specific deployment weren’t disclosed, the SANY SKT105E trucks (the “D” is, presumably, the wide-body variant) the company has deployed elsewhere are powered by a dual-motor electric drivetrain, pairing two permanent-magnet synchronous motors with a dual three-speed automated manual transmission. The system delivers 570 kW (~765 hp) of continuous power and up to 820 kW (~1,100 hp) at peak output, with each motor producing some 2,430 Nm (~18,00 lb-ft) of peak torque.

Those motors get their electrons from an absolute whopper of a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery pack in capacities ranging from 423 to 642 kWh, depending on configuration. The big trucks also offer regenerative braking to recover energy on downhill runs, while their fast-charging system can reportedly charge the battery from 20% to 90% in under an hour.

Breaking: Letter from the Editor-in-Chief: The Good and the Hard of Life on GLP-1s

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that “Years of diets that worked for a couple of months, then gave all the weight back and more.
  • According to recent reports, in June, our brilliant News team published a piece about actor Mayim Bialik and her challenging experience with GLP-1 side effects.
  • Jump forward nearly 4 months; our equally brilliant social media team posts the piece on Facebook, leading with one of Bialik’s quotes from the article: “GLP-1s have helped people in serious need.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that “Years of diets that worked for a couple of months, then gave all the weight back and more. Now the food noise has gone quiet,” a GLP-1 user shared.

According to recent reports, in June, our brilliant News team published a piece about actor Mayim Bialik and her challenging experience with GLP-1 side effects. It did well, like many of the celebrity + health condition + human-interest angle features we create tend to do with our audience (that’s you all reading this!). Not a massive viral hit by any measure, but a strong performer on the traffic front.

Life in a busy newsroom went on.

Jump forward nearly 4 months; our equally brilliant social media team posts the piece on Facebook, leading with one of Bialik’s quotes from the article: “GLP-1s have helped people in serious need. Of that I am certain. But nobody talks much about what happens when it goes wrong.”.

The fuse was lit. Nearly 12k likes, 1k reposts, and 3.5k comments later, the team had their most engaged post of the year by some margin. The irony is not lost on me that Bialik’s quote, about how rarely people talk about side effects, sparked such a deep conversation about that very thing.

Recent findings suggest that GLP-1s are a massive topic for Healthline. They drive traffic, they drive revenue, and they offer a rich seam of human-centric storytelling for our teams. Even so, no one predicted the post would catch fire the way it did. Our social team’s read is that a few things stacked up: Mayim Bialik is a name our Facebook audience knows, the topic is one where nearly everyone has a stake, and a busy thread tends to get shown to more people, who then add more comments. That’s the hypothesis. What we’ve consistently seen is that posts that lead with a quote get more people talking than those that lead with a headline. You may have noticed this article takes the same approach.

We also know that the comment sections on social media aren’t always the most hospitable of environments, particularly in the health space. What stood out about the lion’s share of the comments we read was how constructive the discourse was. People were leading with deeply personal and often moving perspectives about the life changing impact (for good and bad) of GLP-1s. In turn, they were met with equally balanced and thoughtful responses.

Many of the comments expanded on Bialik’s experience, detailing long and difficult battles with a range of side effects. But plenty told the other side of the story: years of failed diets and struggles with chronic conditions leading to despondency, side effects that went on to ease with time, and life changing results that were ultimately worth the cost.

The line that opened this piece could have come from any of those commenters. It didn’t. It came from Kitty Hough, who is 75 and lives in London. Eagle-eyed readers will have spotted that she has the same surname as me – that’s because she’s my mom. She’s one of two people closer to the Healthline home who spoke to me for this piece and whose stories echo the Facebook post thread, with the good and the hard bits side by side.

Kitty was a hockey player and distance runner as a girl, the kind who could eat what she liked without it showing. Then came children, and a weight that crept up year after year, with decades of diets that “worked for a couple of months only to be back to my former weight and then some.” In late 2024, after a lot of research, she decided to try tirzepatide.

Industry observers note that since then, Kitty has lost 56 pounds. She says her joints hurt less, which she puts down to reduced inflammation. She is more mobile. The constant chatter about food has faded. She thinks harder before she eats now.

Industry observers note that “I am a strong believer that obesity is a disease and in my case certainly not the result of overindulgence or laziness,” she notes. “GLP-1s have greatly improved my health and self-esteem. After years of struggling with my weight, I have finally found a way to solve the problem.”.

Kitty will also tell you what it cost. Nausea. Constipation. Sulfur-tasting burps and rough nights of indigestion. Initial hair loss that has since grown back, and loose skin. Muscle loss. And she misses some of the true joy of cooking and eating food.

But despite bumps in her journey, Kitty remains convinced that the benefits of GLP-1s for her life and health outweigh any drawbacks she’s experienced. “I am conscious that I will probably be on this drug for a long time if not for life. It is truly a miracle drug.”.

I also spoke to Ann Marie Maguire, AGNP-C, RN, TCTCN, a nurse practitioner specializing in transplantation and cellular therapy, the sister of Healthline’s Chief Business Officer Christine Macguire, and someone who has lost over 50lbs since starting GLP-1s in 2022.

Recent findings suggest that “I struggled with my weight since my teens and always believed I should be able to manage it on my own. But in my 30s, my knees were hurting just getting out of bed or walking to dinner. I realized how much my weight was affecting my quality of life. Starting a GLP-1 in 2022, alongside healthier eating and exercise, made a tremendous difference. My only regret is not starting sooner,” said Ann Marie.

As a healthcare professional, Ann Marie also identified cost as a major factor that can’t be ignored regarding GLP-1s and their impact.

“There’s understandable debate about the long-term use and cost of these medications,” she indicates. “But we also need to consider the health and financial burden of obesity, including cardiovascular complications, hospitalizations, surgeries and ongoing medications. The cost conversation should account for the potential benefits of preventing or reducing those complications.”.

Recent findings suggest that ann Marie points to a frustration many patients will recognize: reaching a healthier weight can become the reason coverage gets cut off. “We don’t automatically stop blood pressure medication because a patient’s readings improve,” she says. The treatment may be what’s keeping the condition controlled. Obesity, she argues, deserves the same approach. “Reaching a goal weight can mean treatment is working, and decisions about continuing it should reflect the patient’s ongoing needs, benefits and side effects.”.

According to recent reports, it’s vital to note that this article looks at the experiences of only a handful of people out of the millions who now take GLP-1s. Like all drugs, these medications are not right for everyone. Side effects are common; some of them can be serious, and both the long-term impact and what happens when people stop are still being worked out. Ultimately, your care team, with knowledge of your medical history, is a far better guide than a comment thread.

Yet the evidence now reaches well beyond the scales: large trials have linked semaglutide to fewer heart attacks and strokes in people with heart disease and slower kidney decline in people with diabetes and kidney disease, and tirzepatide became the first FDA-approved drug for moderate to severe sleep apnea in adults with obesity.

Sources indicate that stories like Kitty’s, Ann Marie’s, Mayim Bialik’s, and those of the 3.5k commenters on the Facebook post aren’t proof of what will happen to you one way or another. But for a lot of people, my mom included, these drugs have changed what an ordinary day looks like, and in many cases changed what their future can look like.

Industry observers note that one of the most significant drug developments of the century so far? Hard to argue with.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Wednesday in our Healthline Wellness Wire newsletter.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that autonomous lawncare specialists Greenzie passed a major milestone with their self-driving mowers last week, surpassing 255,000 cumulative robomowing miles. For context, that’s far enough to mow every inch of space between the Earth and Moon.

Greenzie revealed the self-driving milestone last week, and it’s genuinely impressive, reflecting Greenzie Powered Autonomy mowing more than 9 billion (with a b) square feet of turf across more than 200 commercial customers, 45 US states, and more than 500,000 equivalent man-hours of mowing.

And, while I might have pointed the fact that Greenzie mowers have covered more miles in its press release than Daimler’s entire hydrogen truck fleet, the organization really seems to be leaning into the Moon angle.

“We mowed to the moon, but the real achievement is the commercial experience behind those miles,” indicates Charles Brian Quinn, co-founder and CEO of Greenzie and almost definitely the guy who first came up with the lunar lawncare line. “Every mile represents equipment working on real properties with commercial crews. That experience has shaped our technology, strengthened our OEM partnerships and taught us how to help customers successfully integrate autonomy into their daily operations.”.

It has been revealed that greenzie develops autonomous packages for, and maintains OEM relationships with electric brands Mean Green Electric Mowers (whose Vanquish Autonomous commercial mower is shown, above), and Greenworks Commercial, as well as gas-powered brands like Bobcat and Wright Manufacturing. Regardless of what powers the mowers, Greenzie supplies the self-driving technology and integration expertise, while its OEM partners develop and manufacture the equipment that does the actual cutting, clearing, and whatever else their clients need.

Sources indicate that “Successful autonomy requires more than capable technology,” said Steve Bush, chief operating officer of Greenzie. “Customers need to understand where autonomy fits into their operations, how to prepare their crews and how to measure success. We have spent years learning those lessons alongside our customers and OEM partners, creating a more consistent path to adoption as the industry grows.”.

The Mean Green Vanquish Autonomous featured gere is a fully electric, stand-on, zero-turn (ZTR) mower built around an all-day-ready 22 kWh li-ion battery pack and featuring a 60″ rear-discharge mulching deck.

Mean Green claims that the combination of big battery and the electric motors that drive the ZTR mower and spin up its blades are good up to eight hours of continuous mowing on a charge, with an aluminum chassis and deck helping to keep the machine’s overall weight down for easier towing maximum efficiency.

The firm says the mower can operate in either manual or autonomous mode, with Greenzie’s self-driving software supported by six depth-sensing stereo cameras providing 360-degree vision, RTK-corrected GPS, and visual-inertial odometry for onboard site mapping and precise positioning, which Greenzie says allows the mower to detect obstacles up to twenty feet away, recognize designated keep-out zones, and automatically return to its starting point when called back.

A top speed of 11.5 mph and the ability to repeat saved mowing routes, the Vanquish is designed to give commercial landscaping crews another productive worker without adding another person to the payroll … which, with a $60,000 asking price, is money they will probably still need.

Let’s get some pro-labor rage going in the comments, and don’t forget to mention what kind of paycheck you’d need to get to go work in landscaping 2,000+ hours a year while you’re there.

THERE IS, PERHAPS, no menswear staple more classic than the wristwatch. Take Koon's gold watch in Pulp Fiction or 007's high-tech timepieces: The best watches for men tell a story and time, while instantly elevating your ensemble. In the watch world, there's a ticker for everyone—whether you're making power moves in the boardroom or chasing the next adventure. Need a leather-strapped dress watch that pairs nicely with your suit? Or maybe you're after a rugged outdoor watch or sports watch to track your laps?

It has been revealed that with many options on the market, finding the right one can feel like diving into a black hole. But don't sweat it—we've tested it all, from everyday essentials to luxury standouts. Whether you're looking to monitor your fitness stats, are after your first watch to wear to the office, need some water-resistance, or have to have dial luminescence in the dark for easy readability, these 7 watches have proven to be the best in style, durability, and function. Step right up, because there's a watch for every guy.

Timex offers the ultimate bang-for-your-buck watch, no question about it. Our testers found it’s the easiest dial to read of all the watch options on this list. That lively blue is sharp enough to catch everyone’s attention but still versatile enough to pair with pretty much any casual or formal fit. It fits comfortably on the wrist and can smoothly adjust if you need to loosen or tighten it. And here’s the kicker: It’s under $100.

Recent findings suggest that yep, you get all this without putting a dent in your wallet—which can be noted for nearly all the watches Timex makes. At the push of the crown, the brand's signature Indiglo light-up feature will take over, which means no squinting to see the time for both daytime strolls and late-night outings. The two-tone silver and brass case and mineral glass crystal keep it durable yet lightweight, so it can handle daily wear. Plus, with 10 different colorways, there are options to match your vibe, whether you want something that is "in your face" or semi-low-key.
